Welcome to the WESPAA Research Lab

The WESPAA Research Lab (Water, Earth, Space, Air and Agni (Fire)) conducts research at the intersection of robotics, security, artificial intelligence and materials. The lab develops robotic systems capable of operating across the full range of physical environments, from underwater and terrestrial settings to aerial, space and high-temperature domains.

Research at the lab is guided by a commitment to methods that are principled, reproducible and experimentally validated. Current projects include ROMER I, a reconfigurable modular robot for planetary exploration and construction, and the Glyph Perturbation Cardinality (GPC) and Quinary Pixel Combination (QPC) frameworks for secure information hiding. The lab's work has been presented at international venues, including DFRWS EU 2026 in Linköping, Sweden, and the ETSI Security Conference 2026 in Sophia Antipolis, France.

Research areas

Security

Methods for protecting and securely embedding data in images and rendered text, with changes that are invisible to the eye and exactly recoverable.

  • GPC: Glyph Perturbation Cardinality
  • QPC: Quinary Pixel Combinations

Robotics

Modular, reconfigurable robots that change their shape and size to move across unstructured terrain and support construction in planetary environments.

  • ROMER I

Research

The lab's projects, grouped by research area.

Security

Security

GPC: Glyph Perturbation Cardinality

Overview

GPC is a raster domain framework for hiding data inside rendered text. Unlike methods that alter the wording or structure of text, it works only after the font has been rasterised, modifying the bitmap produced by a deterministic text rendering pipeline.

Method

  • Each rendered glyph acts as one covert encoding unit.
  • The hidden value is expressed by the number of interior ink pixels that receive a minimal intensity change.
  • These changes are visually imperceptible but form a stable, decodable signal.

Supported data

Demonstrated for text-to-text embedding and extended to images, audio and video by normalising image intensities, audio features and video frame values into bounded integer sequences distributed across glyphs.

Figures

Select a figure to view it full size.

GPC paper series

The GPC research programme is organised around six research questions, from the foundations of glyph-level embedding through to learned and LLM-guided optimisation.

  1. Paper 1
    Foundation of GPC

    Research question: Can textual glyphs be used for steganographic applications?

    Contribution: Glyph viability analysis, font and font-size analysis, perturbation cardinality analysis, information capacity estimation, deterministic embedding, recoverability, and visual fidelity evaluation.

  2. Paper 2
    Machine Learning based GPC Optimisation

    Research question: Can pixel selection within glyph perturbations be optimised using machine learning?

    Contribution: Developed MLP and Graph Transformer approaches for learned pixel selection using spatial and structural glyph features, improving reconstruction quality through higher SSIM/PSNR and reduced MSE.

  3. Paper 3
    Capacity and Robustness Analysis

    Research question: How much information can be embedded within glyphs, and how robust is the approach?

    Contribution: Evaluated embedding capacity across fonts, font sizes, and colour channels, including robustness against compression and format conversion.

  4. Paper 4
    Multimodal GPC Framework

    Research question: Can GPC support multimodal information hiding?

    Contribution: Developed an architecture for embedding image, audio, and video information into textual glyph carriers. The framework demonstrated the capability of embedding a 32×32 image using only five glyphs.

  5. Paper 5
    Cross-language Generalisation

    Research question: Can GPC generalise across different scripts and glyph distributions?

    Contribution: Evaluated the GPC framework using zero-shot learning across multiple font styles and sizes, demonstrating generalisation without extensive retraining.

  6. Paper 6
    LLM-guided Adaptive Steganography Ongoing

    Research question: Can Large Language Models optimise glyph selection and cover-text generation?

    Contribution: Currently investigating the use of LLMs combined with ML-generated ground truth capacity data to generate optimised cover text and allocate glyphs efficiently for improved payload capacity and visual quality.

Security

QPC: Quinary Pixel Combinations

Overview

QPC is a deterministic spatial domain method for hiding text in images. Instead of bit-level substitution spread over several pixels, it encodes one complete character in a single RGB pixel.

Method

  • Each of the R, G and B channels is shifted by one of five levels: −2, −1, 0, +1 or +2.
  • This gives 125 distinct combinations; 98 are mapped to uppercase and lowercase letters, digits, whitespace and common special characters, with 27 reserved for future use.
  • Decoding subtracts the cover image from the stego image and maps each difference back to its character, giving exact recovery.

Robotics

Robotics

ROMER I: Reconfigurable Omnidirectional Modular Elastic Robot

Overview

ROMER I is a conceptual robot for exploration and construction in unstructured planetary environments. Wheeled, tracked and legged robots have fixed mechanical structures once deployed, while soft robots adapt well but carry little load. ROMER I combines both: a rigid internal frame of linear actuators arranged in a cubic lattice, enclosed by a continuous elastic outer membrane.

Figures

Select a figure to view it full size.

Key capabilities

  • Scaling: synchronised extension and contraction of all actuators produces compact, expanded and elongated states of the same frame.
  • Shape change: independent control of selected actuators reshapes the body into cube, cuboid and sphere configurations while keeping the frame connected.
  • Locomotion without wheels: actuators on one side shift the centre of mass beyond the base of support, so the robot tips into a new stable position. Repeating this in sequence produces directional movement.
  • Cooperative operation: multiple units can work together for surveying, transporting materials and forming simple structures.

Applications

Planetary surface exploration over uneven terrain, distributed surveying, and robotic construction in environments without existing infrastructure.

Status

Concept design and CAD model complete.
